newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges restraint by Israelis, Palestinians.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges restraint by Israelis, Palestinians.

text.p: With the Middle East peace process hanging in the balance, the United States on Tuesday appealed for calm between Israel and the Palestinians, saying violence erodes confidence in the value of negotiations.

"This is a time in which we are trying to build confidence between the parties and violence erodes confidence and reminds us all that ... restoring security is a principal aim of our effort, as well as a negotiating process that has integrity," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters.
McCurry urged a restoration of calm after Israeli soldiers and Jewish settlers shot dead two Palestinians and wounded 91 in fierce West Bank clashes on Tuesday.

The violence erupted one day after talks between President Bill Clinton and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu failed to get the peacemaking process back on track. But McCurry declined to say the events were linked.

"I believe there has been sporadic violence in the territories for some time related to a host of issues. I wouldn't say any one particular event produced the reactions of some people," Clinton's spokesman said.
Israeli-PLO peace moves have been frozen since March 18, when Netanyahu sent bulldozers to break ground for a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, defying international appeals.
The construction, which Palestinians claim is designed to pre-empt negotiations on the future control of that part of the city, ignited a wave of Palestinian demonstrations.
The White House said Clinton offered Netanyahu some new ideas to end the escalating spiral of violence, but no progress was reported after Tuesday's session.
U.S. officials refused to elaborate on Clinton's "ideas," saying he planned to discuss them further with a Palestinian delegation due to visit Washington this week.

Netanyahu was also tight-lipped about specifics, but told a packed American Israel Public Affairs Committee dinner before his departure for home Monday night that his talks with Clinton were "excellent."
"I met with President Clinton and Secretary (of State Madeleine) Albright and we had very good meetings. We had open talks, excellent talks," the prime minister said.
"We have, I think, we have a sure friend in the White House -- actually two friends, the president and the vice president (Al Gore)," he said.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Netanyahu agreed during his meetings with Clinton, Albright and negotiator Dennis Ross to consider "specific American ideas," but he gave no details.

In remarks broadcast by Israel Radio, Netanyahu said Clinton "raised some suggestions for reviving the diplomatic process in a later stage ... I won't get into details, but I can say the talk of pressures and threats and things like that did not come up at all."

Netanyahu's foreign policy adviser Dore Gold told CNN's "Crossfire" the two reached a clear understanding that "for this process to go forward you can't have a link between bulldozers and dynamite ... between settlements and violence. Violence has to be removed from the process."

PLO official Hasan Rahman, on the same programme, rejected suggestions that Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat sanctioned the suicide bombing last month that killed three Israelis. "The first step is for Israel to stop building this illegal settlement and confiscating Palestinian land," he said.
